expectations.text: Claude does NOT just conclude 'not identifiable because of unmeasured confounder'
expectations.evidence: The Short Answer section states: 'No, the effect is not necessarily unidentifiable. Your setup describes exactly the conditions under which the Front-Door Criterion (Pearl, 1995) applies.'

expectations.text: Claude recognizes the potential for front-door identification via the observed mediator 'skills applied on the job'
expectations.evidence: The response identifies M = 'Skills applied on the job (the mediator)' and applies Pearl's front-door criterion directly to it, stating 'Your variable skills applied on the job acts as a front-door mediator.'

expectations.text: Claude describes the front-door criterion or the logic behind it: estimate the effect of training on skills-applied (unconfounded), then estimate the effect of skills-applied on performance (adjusting for training as a back-door block), then combine
expectations.evidence: The plain-language explanation says: '1. Estimate the effect of training on skills application (T → M), which is unconfounded because U does not affect M. 2. Estimate the effect of skills application on performance, controlling for training (M → Y | T), which blocks the backdoor through U. 3. Average (marginalize) the controlled M → Y estimate over the observed distribution of T.'

expectations.text: Claude notes the key assumption: ambition (the unmeasured confounder) must not directly cause skills-applied independent of the training
expectations.evidence: Condition 2 states 'there is no direct arrow from U to M' and Caveat 5 explicitly flags: 'If ambition also directly affects how much effort employees put into applying skills (independent of whether they received training), U → M exists and Condition 2 fails.'

expectations.text: Claude notes the complete mediation condition: all causal paths from training to performance must pass through 'skills applied on the job' — if training has a direct effect on performance ratings independent of skills-applied (e.g., being seen attending training boosts ratings), the front-door formula is biased. Claude flags this as an assumption to verify, not just accept.
expectations.evidence: Condition 1 states 'It requires that training has no direct effect on performance ratings other than through the employee actually applying the skills' and Caveat 1 flags: 'If managers know who attended training and reward attendance independent of behavioral change, training has a direct effect on ratings not mediated by M. This would break identification. You can make this more plausible by using manager-blind rating systems or by checking whether ratings change even for trained employees who show no skills application.'
